messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet was thirty-five, an accountant in a mid-sized firm, and divorced for two years. The marriage had unravelled quietly, not from any single blow but from a thousand small distances he could not explain.

Ten years earlier, he had been a student in his home country, arrested at a peaceful protest and taken to a detention centre. For three weeks, interrogators beat him, burned him with cigarettes, and held his head underwater until he gagged. They spoke in the same language as the neighbours he had known his whole life, which made the betrayal feel absolute. When he was finally released in a prisoner exchange, he fled to the United States. He told no one the details, not even his wife. He had come to believe that speaking about it would prove what he already suspected: that he was permanently changed for the worse, that the man who had been tortured was someone else, not the person who now sat in a cubicle staring at spreadsheets.

That belief—that the memory belonged to a stranger—was reinforced every time the past crashed into the present. A sudden memory would arrive like a film playing over and over, but the scenes were scrambled: the sting of a cigarette burn before the smell of wet concrete, the sound of a door slamming after the feeling of his handcuffs tightening. He could never put the order right, and the confusion made the memory feel even more alien, as though it had been implanted in his mind by someone else.

The triggers were everywhere, though he tried not to notice. A stranger approaching him on the street would make his chest tighten. He would immediately scan the man’s hands, his jacket, the way he walked—searching for a hidden weapon. Those few seconds of scanning shifted something inside Kiet: he began to think that this person, whoever he was, could harm him without warning. *You can never know who will harm you* became a silent mantra. And that thought, in turn, would drag the worst memory back into his mind—the first time an interrogator had smiled before hitting him. The loop was fast and invisible: a stranger triggered the fear of harm, and that fear triggered the memory replay.

At work, Kiet was efficient and quiet. He avoided talking about the future with colleagues because every conversation about next year or a promotion felt like a trap. What was the point of planning when someone could take it all away? When a client asked him over the phone about his goals for the quarter, Kiet would feel the familiar dread rise, and then the memory would flicker—the cold concrete floor, the smell of his own sweat—and he would go silent. He had also come to believe, bitterly, that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening. A stronger person would have fought back, would have said the right thing. That appraisal made him feel weak and irreparably broken, and the feeling of being broken made the memories feel even more unreal, as though they could not possibly belong to him.

The divorce had been a quiet dissolution. His wife had said he was distant, that he never talked about how he felt, that she could not reach him. He knew she was right, but he could not find a way to explain that he himself could not reach the part of him that had lived through those weeks. That part felt sealed away, and yet it kept leaking out.

What finally brought Kiet to a clinic was a panic attack during a routine meeting. A new manager, an older man, had asked him casually, “So, Kiet, where do you see yourself in five years?” The question landed like a blow. Kiet excused himself, locked the bathroom stall, and struggled to breathe. His boss later suggested he talk to someone. Kiet agreed because he was afraid—not of the panic, but of what it confirmed: that he was permanently damaged, that no amount of time could put the film in order, and that the man who had been tortured was still inside him, waiting for the next trigger. He came to the first session not knowing what he hoped for, only knowing he could no longer pretend the film was not playing.
